title: [2501.19195] Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate

sections.heading: Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate

content.text: Machine learning classifiers often produce probabilistic predictions that are critical for accurate and interpretable decision-making in various domains. The quality of these predictions is generally evaluated with proper losses like cross-entropy, which decompose into two components: *calibration error* assesses general under/overconfidence, while *refinement error* measures the ability to distinguish different classes. In this paper, we provide theoretical and empirical evidence that these two errors are not minimized simultaneously during training. Selecting the best training epoch based on validation loss thus leads to a compromise point that is suboptimal for both calibration error and, most importantly, refinement error. To address this, we introduce a new metric for early stopping and hyperparameter tuning that makes it possible to minimize refinement error during training. The calibration error is minimized after training, using standard techniques. Our method integrates seamlessly with any architecture and consistently improves performance across diverse classification tasks.
![Refer to caption](./[2501.19195] Rethinking Early Stopping_ Refine, Then Calibrate_files/x1.png)

Accurate classification lies at the heart of many machine learning applications, from medical diagnosis to autonomous driving systems. Modern classifiers predict not only a class label but also a probability vector reflecting the model’s confidence that the instance belongs to each class. This probabilistic output is critical for downstream decision-making. Despite their widespread use, many machine learning models, especially complex ones such as neural networks, tend to produce poorly calibrated probabilities (Guo et al., [2017](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib26)), meaning that the predicted confidence does not align with real-world probabilities.

This issue has mostly been considered through the lens of post-hoc calibration, which consists in adjusting the predicted probabilities after training, using a small held-out portion of the dataset. An overlooked aspect of the problem is that the calibration error contributes to the total loss of a classifier (Bröcker, [2009](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib9)). In [Figure 1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#S1.F1 "In 1 Introduction ‣ Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate") we plot the decomposition of the classification loss (here cross-entropy) into calibration error and refinement error during training for a deep neural network. We observe that the two are not minimized simultaneously. The resulting validation loss minimizer thus has a non-zero calibration error and is suboptimal for refinement. This observation reveals that there is room for improvement in the way we train machine learning classifiers.

In Sections [2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#S2 "2 Calibration-Refinement decomposition ‣ Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate") and [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#S3 "3 Our method: refinement-based stopping ‣ Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate") we propose minimizing only the refinement error during training and the calibration error after training. This new paradigm can be used seamlessly with any machine learning model by simply using our new refinement estimator, provided in the package [github.com/dholzmueller/probmetrics](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/github.com/dholzmueller/probmetrics), as a stopping metric. In [Section 4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#S4 "4 Experiments ‣ Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate"), we present empirical evidence of the loss reduction achieved across various problems. In Sections [5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#S5 "5 Decomposition in the Gaussian data model ‣ Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate") and [6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#S6 "6 High dimensional asymptotics of logistic regression ‣ Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate"), we study logistic regression on a binary Gaussian data model, demonstrating that the problem exists even in simple settings and that our method minimizes both refinement and calibration errors.

We begin by overviewing the decomposition of proper losses into calibration and refinement errors. We also present a new variational formulation of this decomposition that allows a reinterpretation of refinement as the loss after optimal post-processing.

Consider classification with kk classes. We make probabilistic predictions p∈Δkp\in\Delta\_{k} on the value of the true label YY using a statistical model f:ℝp→Δkf:\mathbb{R}^{p}\rightarrow\Delta\_{k}.

We use the same notation to denote the expected loss obtained when making prediction pp: ℓ​(p,q)=𝔼y∼q​[ℓ​(p,y)]\ell(p,q)=\mathbb{E}\_{y\sim q}[\ell(p,y)]. The first term in the decomposition ([1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#S2.E1 "Equation 1 ‣ 2.1 Proper loss decomposition ‣ 2 Calibration-Refinement decomposition ‣ Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate")) is the calibration error 𝒦ℓ​(f)\mathcal{K}\_{\ell}(f) associated with ℓ\ell. The second term, denoted ℛℓ​(f)\mathcal{R}\_{\ell}(f), is the refinement error for ℓ\ell. Refinement error is sometimes further decomposed into the irreducible loss (risk of the optimal classifier f∗f^{\*}), and the grouping loss (Kull & Flach, [2015](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib32); Perez-Lebel et al., [2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib48)).

Calibration has received a lot of attention on its own, not always in the context of the calibration-refinement decomposition. A model ff is said to be calibrated if f​(X)=Cf(X)=C almost surely. When this is satisfied, for a given prediction f​(X)=pf(X)=p, the expected outcome C=𝔼​[Y|f​(X)]C=\mathbb{E}[Y|f(X)] is aligned with pp. This is a desirable property in that it makes model predictions interpretable as probabilities that YY belongs to each of the kk classes.

Model mis-calibration is thus measured by the expected gap between f​(X)f(X) and CC. The choice of a distance or divergence function dd gives rise to different notions of *calibration error*: 𝒦(d)​(f)=𝔼​[d​(f​(X),C)]\mathcal{K}^{(d)}(f)=\mathbb{E}[d(f(X),C)]. A popular choice for dd is the L1L^{1} distance, resulting in the expected calibration error (ECE, Naeini et al., [2015](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib42)). Note that when picking the L2L^{2} distance or KL divergence, we recover “proper” calibration errors (Gruber & Buettner, [2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib23)), that appear in the decomposition of the Brier score and the logloss. In practice, the data distribution 𝒟\mathcal{D} is only known via a finite set of samples (xi,yi)1≤i≤n(x\_{i},y\_{i})\_{1\leq i\leq n} and ff makes continuous predictions f​(xi)∈Δkf(x\_{i})\in\Delta\_{k}. To compute the calibration error, CC is often estimated by binning predictions on the simplex, resulting in estimators that are biased and inconsistent (Kumar et al., [2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib35); Vaicenavicius et al., [2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib57); Roelofs et al., [2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib52)). In the multi-class case, the curse of dimensionality makes estimation even more difficult. Weaker notions like class-wise or top-label calibration error are often used (Kumar et al., [2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib35); Kull et al., [2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib34)).

Many machine learning classifiers suffer from calibration issues, which gave rise to a family of techniques known as “post hoc calibration.” These methods reduce calibration error after training using a reserved set of samples 𝒞\mathcal{C} called a “calibration set.” Among others, isotonic regression and temperature scaling are widely used.

Isotonic regression (IR, Zadrozny & Elkan, [2002](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib61)) finds the monotonic function g∗g^{\*} that minimizes the risk of g∘fg\circ f on the calibration set. It is a popular calibration technique for binary classifiers. The multi-class extensions come with important drawbacks however.

Temperature scaling (TS, Guo et al., [2017](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib26)) optimizes a scalar parameter β\beta to rescale the log-probabilities. Formally, it learns the function gβ∗g\_{\beta^{\*}} on the calibration set with {IEEEeqnarray\*}+rCl+x\* g\_β(p) & ≔ softmax(βlog(p)), β^\* ≔ argmin\_β∈R\_+ L(β), L(β) ≔ ∑\_(x, y) ∈C ℓ(g\_β(f(x)), y) . \IEEEyesnumber For neural networks, this comes down to rescaling the last layer by β∗\beta^{\*}. TS has many advantages: it is efficient, applies to multi-class problems, does not affect accuracy, and is robust to overfitting since it only has one parameter.

We refer the interested reader to Silva Filho et al. ([2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib55)) for a detailed review of calibration. In [Appendix A](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#A1 "Appendix A Related work ‣ Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate") we also take a closer look at the literature on the subject and other related works.

Given the appeal of calibrated predictions, significant effort has been devoted to estimating and reducing calibration error. The fact that it interacts with another term to form the overall risk of the classifier, however, has received much less attention. This is partly due to the fact that refinement error is little known. So what exactly is refinement?

In decomposition ([1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#S2.E1 "Equation 1 ‣ 2.1 Proper loss decomposition ‣ 2 Calibration-Refinement decomposition ‣ Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate")), it appears as the expected ℓ\ell-entropy of YY given f​(X)f(X): ℛℓ​(f)=𝔼​[eℓ​(𝔼​[Y|f​(X)])]\mathcal{R}\_{\ell}(f)=\mathbb{E}[e\_{\ell}(\mathbb{E}[Y|f(X)])]. With simple intuition about entropy functions, we see that if YY is fully determined by f​(X)f(X), Y|f​(X)Y|f(X) has no entropy and the refinement error is null. In contrast, if Y|f​(X)Y|f(X) is as random as YY, it is maximal. Refinement error thus quantifies how much of the variability in YY is captured by f​(X)f(X), with a lower error indicating greater information. Just like classification error, it assesses the ability to distinguish between classes independently of calibration issues like over/under-confidence. It provides a much more comprehensive measure, however, as it considers the entire distribution of f​(X)f(X) rather than a single discretization. This comes at the cost that, like calibration error, it is much harder to estimate.

In Appendix [B](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#A2 "Appendix B Calibration, Refinement, and Sharpness ‣ Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate") we introduce novel variational formulations of the terms in decomposition ([1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#S2.E1 "Equation 1 ‣ 2.1 Proper loss decomposition ‣ 2 Calibration-Refinement decomposition ‣ Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate")), most importantly:
The refinement error for proper loss ℓ\ell is
where the minimum is taken over all measurable functions g:Δk→Δkg:\Delta\_{k}\rightarrow\Delta\_{k}. It is attained at g∗​(f​(X))=𝔼​[Y|f​(X)]g^{\*}(f(X))=\mathbb{E}[Y|f(X)].

Calibration error evaluates how much the population risk can be reduced by optimally re-labeling the original forecasts. This optimal relabeling is given by the calibrated score C=𝔼​[Y|f​(X)]C=\mathbb{E}[Y|f(X)]. This is quite intuitive: such re-labeling sets the calibration error to zero, leaving only the refinement term in the risk decomposition ([1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#S2.E1 "Equation 1 ‣ 2.1 Proper loss decomposition ‣ 2 Calibration-Refinement decomposition ‣ Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate")). Refinement error thus measures the remaining risk after optimal re-labeling, which corresponds to the risk of the calibrated scores. This new variational formulation reveals that refinement error can be estimated using the risk after post-hoc calibration.

Minimizing the risk of a classifier comes down to minimizing simultaneously refinement and calibration errors. Empirically, these two errors are not minimized simultaneously during training, as in [Figure 1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#S1.F1 "In 1 Introduction ‣ Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate"). One possible scenario is that the training set becomes well separated, forcing the model to make very confident predictions to keep training calibration error small. In case of a train-test generalization gap, the model becomes over-confident (Carrell et al., [2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib11)) while refinement error might still decrease. We observe separate minimizers across various machine learning models, whether through iterative training or when tuning a regularization parameter. In [Section 6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#S6 "6 High dimensional asymptotics of logistic regression ‣ Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate"), we analyze this phenomenon theoretically for high-dimensional logistic regression, showing it appears even in very simple settings. The consequence is that risk-based early stopping finds a compromise point between two conflicting objectives: calibration error minimization and refinement error minimization. This corroborates the widely recognized observation that many models are poorly calibrated after training (Guo et al., [2017](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib26)).

The question that arises is: how do we get a model optimal for both calibration and refinement? In general, strictly increasing post hoc calibration techniques like TS leaves refinement unchanged. Berta et al. ([2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib3)) showed that binary IR preserves the ROC convex hull, a proxy for refinement. Given that calibration error is minimized after training, with no impact on refinement, we argue that training should be dedicated to the latter only. We propose selecting the best epoch based on validation refinement error instead of validation loss as a new training paradigm for machine learning classifiers. As illustrated in Figure [2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3 Our method: refinement-based stopping ‣ Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate") this procedure leads to smaller loss after post-hoc calibration. Compared with the standard paradigm that minimizes both refinement and calibration during training, we propose refining during training, then calibrating post hoc.

As discussed earlier, calibration error estimators are biased, inconsistent, and break in the multi-class case. Since refinement is risk minus calibration, these issues carry over to refinement estimation. One could circumvent this by using proxies like validation accuracy. Theorem [2.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#S2.Thmtheorem1 "Theorem 2.1. ‣ 2.4 A variational formulation ‣ 2 Calibration-Refinement decomposition ‣ Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate") provides a better alternative: refinement error equals risk after optimal relabeling g∗∘fg^{\*}\circ f. We thus need to estimate how small the validation risk can get by re-labeling predictions. Since the validation set (xi,yi)1≤i≤n(x\_{i},y\_{i})\_{1\leq i\leq n} is finite, minimizing over all measurable functions g:Δk→Δkg:\Delta\_{k}\rightarrow\Delta\_{k} would lead to drastic overfitting. However, given a class of functions 𝒢\mathcal{G} that we intend to use for post hoc calibration, we can estimate refinement error by solving:

after every epoch. This comes down to early stopping based on validation “loss after post hoc calibration,” which is a biased estimator of refinement error. Compared with [Theorem 2.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#S2.Thmtheorem1 "Theorem 2.1. ‣ 2.4 A variational formulation ‣ 2 Calibration-Refinement decomposition ‣ Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate"), we limit ourselves to functions in class 𝒢\mathcal{G}. A trade-off arises vis-a-vis the size of 𝒢\mathcal{G}. The larger the class the less biased our estimator but the more prone we are to overfitting the validation set, resulting in poor estimation of the true refinement error. For our method to work, we need to choose a small class 𝒢\mathcal{G} that comes as close as possible to the optimal re-mapping g∗​(f)=𝔼​[Y|f​(X)]g^{\*}(f)=\mathbb{E}[Y|f(X)].

We call TS-refinement the estimator obtained when 𝒢\mathcal{G} is the class of functions generated by temperature scaling. It is parametrized by a single scalar parameter, seriously limiting the capacity to over-fit the validation set. Moreover, TS is very effective at reducing the calibration error of neural networks (however large it is) while leaving refinement unchanged. This is supported by a plethora of empirical evidence (Guo et al., [2017](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib26); Wang et al., [2021](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib59)). We demonstrate in [Section 5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#S5 "5 Decomposition in the Gaussian data model ‣ Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate") that under assumptions on the logit distribution, the optimal re-mapping g∗g^{\*} is attained by TS, making TS-refinement an unbiased estimator. In practice, when training a neural network, we recommend selecting the best epoch in terms of validation loss after temperature scaling. Going back to the example in [Figure 1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#S1.F1 "In 1 Introduction ‣ Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate"), this procedure would select a later epoch (red dot), for which validation loss (green curve) is higher but validation loss after TS (red curve) is smaller. Since we were to use TS for post hoc calibration anyway, this simple procedure guarantees a smaller validation risk.

Using TS-refinement for early stopping requires a fast and robust temperature-scaling implementation. Surveying existing codebases made it clear that there is significant room for improvement in terms of both speed and performance. For the logloss, the objective ℒ​(β)\mathcal{L}(\beta) in equation ([2.2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2 "Post hoc calibration. ‣ 2.2 Calibration error ‣ 2 Calibration-Refinement decomposition ‣ Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate")) is convex. Existing implementations apply L-BFGS (Liu & Nocedal, [1989](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib36)) to optimize ℒ​(1/T)\mathcal{L}(1/T), which is unimodal but nonconvex. Additionally, the step-size choice for L-BFGS sometimes led to suboptimal performance. Instead, since ℒ′\mathcal{L}^{\prime} is increasing by convexity of ℒ\mathcal{L}, we propose using bisection to find a zero of ℒ′\mathcal{L}^{\prime}. [Figure 3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#S3.F3 "In TS-refinement for neural nets. ‣ 3.2 Refinement-based stopping made practical ‣ 3 Our method: refinement-based stopping ‣ Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate") shows that on the benchmark from [Section 4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#S4 "4 Experiments ‣ Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate"), our implementation achieves lower test loss and is significantly faster than alternatives from Guo et al. ([2017](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib26)), TorchUncertainty, and AutoGluon (Erickson et al., [2020](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib17)). We provide details in Appendix [E](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#A5 "Appendix E Temperature scaling implementation and TS-refinement ‣ Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate").

Our method applies to a wide range of machine learning models. It can help select the best step in any iterative training procedure (e.g, boosting) or the amount of regularization for non-iterative models. Refinement does not have to be estimated with TS-refinement, any proxy available can be selected. For non-neural nets, TS can be less effective. In the binary setting, using risk after isotonic regression (IR-refinement) might be a good option. It is much less biased than TS-refinement since the class 𝒢\mathcal{G} contains all monotonic functions. The risk of overfitting gets larger however and must be considered carefully.

We benchmark our method by training a ResNet-18 (He et al., [2016](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib27)) and WideResNet (WRN) (Zagoruyko, [2016](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib62)) on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and SVHN datasets (Krizhevsky et al., [2009](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib31); Netzer et al., [2011](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib43)). We reserve 10% of the training set for validation. We train for 300 epochs using SGD with momentum, weight decay, and a step learning rate scheduler. We use random cropping, horizontal flips, and cutout (DeVries, [2017](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib15)). For reference, this training procedures allows us to reach 95%95\% accuracy on CIFAR-10 with the ResNet-18 and over 96%96\% with the WRN. We train the models ten times on each dataset. The code to run the benchmark is available at [github.com/eugeneberta/RefineThenCalibrate-Vision](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/github.com/eugeneberta/RefineThenCalibrate-Vision). On NVIDIA V100 GPUs, the benchmark took around 300 GPU hours to run. We report in [Figure 4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#S3.F4 "In Other estimators. ‣ 3.2 Refinement-based stopping made practical ‣ 3 Our method: refinement-based stopping ‣ Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate") the relative differences in test logloss obtained with different training procedures. After early stopping on validation loss (first column), using TS results in significant improvement (second column). Early stopping on TS-refinement instead of validation loss leads to even better results (third column). We also compare with validation accuracy based early stopping (fourth column), another refinement proxy, showing that TS-refinement more consistently yields smaller loss.

We observed empirically that the learning rate scheduler and regularization strength have an influence on the behavior of calibration error during training. This has consequences on the effect observed with our method. In general though, validation TS-refinement remains the best estimator available for test loss after temperature scaling. Brier score, another proper loss, is less sensitive than logloss to sharp variations in calibration error and can be a good alternative for early stopping for practitioners who want to avoid fitting TS every epoch. We refer the interested reader to Appendix [F](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#A6 "Appendix F Computer vision experiments ‣ Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate") for details on our training procedure and complete results.

Tabular data, where XX is a vector of heterogeneous numerical and/or categorical features, is ubiquitous in ML applications. We take 196 binary and multi-class classification datasets from the benchmark by Ye et al. ([2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib60)), containing between 1K and 100K samples after subsampling the largest datasets, see [Appendix G](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#A7 "Appendix G Tabular experiments ‣ Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate"). We evaluate three methods:

* • XGBoost (Chen & Guestrin, [2016](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib12)) is a popular implementation of gradient-boosted decision trees, with strong performance on tabular benchmarks (Grinsztajn et al., [2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib22)). Due to its iterative optimization, early stopping is relevant for XGBoost as well. * • MLP is a simple multilayer perceptron, similar to the popular MLP baseline by Gorishniy et al. ([2021](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib21)). * • RealMLP (Holzmüller et al., [2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib28)) is a recent state-of-the-art deep learning model for tabular data (Ye et al., [2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib60)), improving the standard MLP in many aspects.

XGBoost (Chen & Guestrin, [2016](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib12)) is a popular implementation of gradient-boosted decision trees, with strong performance on tabular benchmarks (Grinsztajn et al., [2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib22)). Due to its iterative optimization, early stopping is relevant for XGBoost as well.
MLP is a simple multilayer perceptron, similar to the popular MLP baseline by Gorishniy et al. ([2021](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib21)).

RealMLP (Holzmüller et al., [2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib28)) is a recent state-of-the-art deep learning model for tabular data (Ye et al., [2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib60)), improving the standard MLP in many aspects.

For each dataset, we report the mean loss over five random splits into 64% training, 16% validation, and 20% test data. For each split, we run 30 random hyperparameter configurations and select the one with the best validation score. The validation set is also used for stopping and post-hoc calibration. Computations took around 40 hours on a 32-core CPU (for XGBoost) and four RTX 3090 GPUs (for NNs).

[Figure 5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#S4.F5 "In Computer Vision. ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate") shows the results on datasets with at least 10K samples. Generally, we observe that TS as well as stopping/tuning on TS-Refinement helps on most datasets, while stopping on accuracy often yields poor logloss even after TS. Our extended analysis in [Appendix G](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#A7 "Appendix G Tabular experiments ‣ Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate") shows that results are more noisy and unclear for small or easy datasets. However, stopping on TS-Refinement frequently yields better accuracy and AUC than stopping on logloss, and hence strikes an excellent balance between different metrics.

children.heading: 5 Decomposition in the Gaussian data model

content.text: In this section and the next, we embark on a theoretical analysis that provides insight into the calibration-refinement decomposition. We demonstrate that even with a simple data model and predictor, calibration and refinement errors are not minimized simultaneously. This highlights the relevance of refinement-based early stopping and underscores the broad impact of the problem we address.

We use the following stylized model. Consider the feature and label random variables X∈ℝp,Y∈{−1,1}X\in\mathbb{R}^{p},Y\in\{-1,1\} under the two-class Gaussian model X∼𝒩​(μ,Σ)X\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\Sigma) if Y=1Y=1 and X∼𝒩​(−μ,Σ)X\sim\mathcal{N}(-\mu,\Sigma) if Y=−1Y=-1 for some mean μ∈ℝp\mu\in\mathbb{R}^{p} and covariance Σ∈ℝp×p\Sigma\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times p}. We further assume balanced classes, ℙ​(Y=1)=ℙ​(Y=−1)=12\mathbb{P}(Y=1)=\mathbb{P}(Y=-1)=\frac{1}{2}. Under this data model, ℙ​(Y=1|X=x)=σ​(w∗⊤​x)\mathbb{P}(Y=1|X=x)=\sigma({w^{\*}}^{\top}x) with w∗=2​Σ−1​μw^{\*}=2\Sigma^{-1}\mu and σ​(x)=11+e−x\sigma(x)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-x}} denotes the sigmoid function. The sigmoid function’s shape is well suited to describe the posterior probability of YY given XX. Note that this holds for any pair P​(X|Y=±1)P(X|Y=\pm 1) from the same exponential family (Jordan, [1995](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib29)). Proofs for this section are deferred to [Appendix C](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#A3 "Appendix C Proofs for Section 5 ‣ Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate").

We are interested in the calibration and refinement errors of the linear model f​(x)=σ​(w⊤​x)f(x)=\sigma(w^{\top}x). The weight vector ww can be learned with techniques such as logistic regression or linear discriminant analysis (Fisher, [1936](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib19)). Denoting aw=⟨w,w∗⟩Σ/‖w‖Σa\_{w}=\langle w,w^{\*}\rangle\_{\Sigma}/\|w\|\_{\Sigma} with ⟨w,w∗⟩Σ=w⊤​Σ​w∗\langle w,w^{\*}\rangle\_{\Sigma}=w^{\top}\Sigma w^{\*} and ‖w‖Σ=w⊤​Σ​w\|w\|\_{\Sigma}=\sqrt{w^{\top}\Sigma w}, the error rate of the linear model writes err⁡(w)=Φ​(−aw2)\operatorname{err}(w)=\Phi(-\frac{a\_{w}}{2}) where Φ​(x)=12​π​∫−∞xexp⁡(−t22)​𝑑t\Phi(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int\_{-\infty}^{x}\exp(-\frac{t^{2}}{2})dt is the cumulative distribution function of the standard normal distribution. Notice that awa\_{w} is invariant by rescaling of ww. It measures the alignment with the best model w∗w^{\*} independently of the weight vector’s norm. We refer to awa\_{w} as the “expertise level” of our model ff. Interestingly, awa\_{w} also appears in the calibration and refinement errors for this simple model.
For proper loss ℓ\ell, the calibration and refinement errors of our model are
where the expectation is taken on z∼𝒩​(0,1)z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1).

Notice that the refinement error is a decreasing function of awa\_{w}, just like the error rate. Moreover, it depends on ww via awa\_{w} only and so it is invariant by rescaling of the weight vector. In contrast, calibration error is not invariant by rescaling ww. It is minimized, and reaches zero, when ‖w‖Σ=aw\|w\|\_{\Sigma}=a\_{w}. The larger the norm of the weight vector ‖w‖Σ\|w\|\_{\Sigma}, the larger the predicted probabilities σ​(w⊤​x)\sigma(w^{\top}x), so ‖w‖Σ\|w\|\_{\Sigma} can be interpreted as the model’s “confidence level.” The model is calibrated when this confidence level equals the expertise level awa\_{w}. A consequence is that there always exists a rescaling of the weight vector for which the calibration error cancels.

The re-scaled weight vector ws←s​ww\_{s}\leftarrow sw with s=⟨w,w∗⟩Σ/‖w‖Σ2s=\langle w,w^{\*}\rangle\_{\Sigma}/\|w\|\_{\Sigma}^{2} yields null calibration error 𝒦​(ws)=0\mathcal{K}(w\_{s})=0 while preserving the refinement error ℛ​(ws)=ℛ​(w)\mathcal{R}(w\_{s})=\mathcal{R}(w).

Note that such rescaling of the weight vector exactly corresponds to temperature scaling. For classifiers like logistic regression or neural nets that use a sigmoid to produce probabilities, [Theorem 5.2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#S5.Thmtheorem2 "Theorem 5.2. ‣ 5 Decomposition in the Gaussian data model ‣ Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate") establishes that, under the assumption that the logit distribution is a mixture of Gaussians, TS sets calibration error to zero while preserving refinement. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first theoretical guarantee for temperature scaling. An immediate corollary of this and [Theorem 2.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#S2.Thmtheorem1 "Theorem 2.1. ‣ 2.4 A variational formulation ‣ 2 Calibration-Refinement decomposition ‣ Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate") is that refinement error equals risk after temperature scaling: ℛ​(w)=mins∈ℝ⁡Risk⁡(s​w)\mathcal{R}(w)=\min\_{s\in\mathbb{R}}\operatorname{Risk}(sw).

For non-centered or imbalanced data, adding an intercept parameter to TS is necessary to achieve the same result. A similar analysis can be derived for the multi-class case, leading to post-hoc calibration with matrix scaling.

This supports the idea that we should minimize refinement during training. Rescaling the weight vector to the correct confidence level is enough to remove the calibration error after training. From our analysis, it seems clear that calibration and refinement error minimizers do not have to match. The confidence level ‖w‖Σ\|w\|\_{\Sigma} is not constrained to equal the expertise awa\_{w} in any way. We observed empirically that loss and refinement minimizers can be separated. Can we push the analysis further to exhibit this theoretically?

children.heading: 6 High dimensional asymptotics of logistic regression

content.text: In this section, we place ourselves in the setting of regularized logistic regression to study the impact of calibration and refinement on the risk during training. Proofs and missing technical details are provided in [Appendix D](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#A4 "Appendix D Proofs for Section 6 ‣ Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate").
![Refer to caption](./[2501.19195] Rethinking Early Stopping_ Refine, Then Calibrate_files/x7.png)

Consider nn pairs (xi,yi)1≤i≤n(x\_{i},y\_{i})\_{1\leq i\leq n} from the bimodal data model of [Section 5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#S5 "5 Decomposition in the Gaussian data model ‣ Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate") and wλw\_{\lambda} the weight vector learned by solving regularized logistic regression
for a given regularization strength λ∈ℝ+\lambda\in\mathbb{R}\_{+}.

To simplify the formulas, we assume that Σ\Sigma is diagonal. We further assume its eigenvalues (σi)1≤i≤p(\sigma\_{i})\_{1\leq i\leq p} are sampled i.i.d. from a positive, bounded spectral distribution FF. Mai et al. To compute calibration and refinement errors that appear in [Theorem 5.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#S5.Thmtheorem1 "Theorem 5.1. ‣ 5 Decomposition in the Gaussian data model ‣ Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate"), we are interested in ⟨wλ,w∗⟩Σ\langle w\_{\lambda},w^{\*}\rangle\_{\Sigma} and ‖wλ‖Σ\|w\_{\lambda}\|\_{\Sigma}.
where the convergence is in probability.

Results from Dobriban & Wager ([2018](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib16)) allow to derive similar results for regularized LDA and Ridge, leading to simpler formulations of refinement and calibration errors. We omit these results for space constraints.
The data separability parameter cc is hard to interpret; instead, we work with e∗e^{\*}, the error rate of the optimal classifier w∗w^{\*}.

e∗e^{\*} provides a common and interpretable scale for the problem difficulty, whatever the shape of the spectral distribution. Given a spectral distribution FF, [Proposition 6.3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#S6.Thmtheorem3 "Proposition 6.3. ‣ 6 High dimensional asymptotics of logistic regression ‣ Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate") gives a simple relation between e∗e^{\*} and cc. We can choose any bounded and positive distribution FF in our formulas to compute ⟨wλ,w∗⟩Σ\langle w\_{\lambda},w^{\*}\rangle\_{\Sigma} and ‖wλ‖Σ2\|w\_{\lambda}\|\_{\Sigma}^{2}. We pick σ=ε+B​(α,β)\sigma=\varepsilon+B(\alpha,\beta) where BB denotes a Beta distribution with shape parameters (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) and ε\varepsilon is a small shift parameter to make FF strictly positive (given that e∗e^{\*} is always finite, we fix ε=10−3\varepsilon=10^{-3}). This allows us to explore a variety of spectral distribution shapes with a single mathematical model, by tweaking α\alpha and β\beta. Using Propositions [6.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#S6.Thmtheorem1 "Proposition 6.1. ‣ 6 High dimensional asymptotics of logistic regression ‣ Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate") and [6.3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#S6.Thmtheorem3 "Proposition 6.3. ‣ 6 High dimensional asymptotics of logistic regression ‣ Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate"), we obtain formulas for ⟨wλ,w∗⟩Σ,‖wλ‖Σ2\langle w\_{\lambda},w^{\*}\rangle\_{\Sigma},\|w\_{\lambda}\|\_{\Sigma}^{2} and e∗e^{\*}, see [Appendix D](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#A4 "Appendix D Proofs for Section 6 ‣ Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate").

For a given regularization strength λ\lambda, dimensions to samples ratio rr, optimal error rate e∗e^{\*} and spectral distribution FF (controlled by α,β\alpha,\beta), we can compute η,τ,γ\eta,\tau,\gamma by solving the system provided by Mai et al. ([2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib37)). Using [Proposition 6.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#S6.Thmtheorem1 "Proposition 6.1. ‣ 6 High dimensional asymptotics of logistic regression ‣ Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate") and [Theorem 5.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#S5.Thmtheorem1 "Theorem 5.1. ‣ 5 Decomposition in the Gaussian data model ‣ Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate") we obtain the calibration and refinement errors. We provide a fast implementation of this method at [github.com/eugeneberta/RefineThenCalibrate-Theory](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/github.com/eugeneberta/RefineThenCalibrate-Theory). For a fixed set of parameters F,r,e∗F,r,e^{\*}, we can plot a learning curve for logistic regression by varying the amount of regularization λ\lambda. We observe the contributions of calibration and refinement errors to the total logloss of the model, as in [Figure 6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#S6.F6 "In 6 High dimensional asymptotics of logistic regression ‣ Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate").

In this example, calibration and refinement errors are not minimized jointly, resulting in a loss minimizer somewhere between the two that is suboptimal for both errors. Given that we can easily set the calibration error to zero ([Theorem 5.2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#S5.Thmtheorem2 "Theorem 5.2. ‣ 5 Decomposition in the Gaussian data model ‣ Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate")), our mathematical model predicts that refinement-based early stopping yields a 2%2\% decrease in downstream cross-entropy on this example.

We can explore the impact of problem parameters on this phenomenon. We investigate three spectral distribution shapes (first row). For each of these, we plot in [Figure 7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#S6.F7 "In 6 High dimensional asymptotics of logistic regression ‣ Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate") the gap between the calibration error minimizer and the refinement error minimizer (second row) and the relative cross-entropy gains (%\%) obtained when stopping on refinement instead of loss (third row) as a function of the ratio r=p/nr=p/n (x-axis) and problem difficulty e∗e^{\*} (y-axis).
![Refer to caption](./[2501.19195] Rethinking Early Stopping_ Refine, Then Calibrate_files/x8.png)

To interpret spectral distribution shapes, note that a small eigenvalue translates to a small “within class variance” and thus more separable data on the corresponding axis. Smaller eigenvalues correspond to more informative features. The left column depicts a scenario where most features are equally informative. The central column has a wide spread of good and bad features. In the right column, most features are bad while there are a few “hidden” good components. In the first scenario, calibration converges earlier almost everywhere on the parameter space, this corresponds to the regime we observe in computer vision. When informative features are scarce on the other hand, refinement is minimized earlier (right column). This might affect practical settings like genomics or histopathology. When the spectral distribution is more balanced, we see both scenarios co-existing, depending on problem parameters. Refinement-based early stopping always yields smaller loss, in the regions where the two minimizers are far apart (whichever error is minimized first), the gains are drastic with up to 25%25\% loss decrease.

Bartlett et al. ([2020](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib2)) establish that benign overfitting occurs for linear regression in a similar data model under some condition on the spectral distribution of the covariance matrix. An avenue for future work is to study how this translates to classification and the link with the calibration-refinement decomposition.

We have demonstrated that selecting the best epoch and hyperparameters based on refinement error solves an issue that arises when using the validation loss. We established that refinement error can be estimated by the loss after post hoc calibration. This allowed us to use TS-refinement for early stopping, yielding improvement in test loss on various machine learning problems. Our estimator is available in the probmetrics package [github.com/dholzmueller/probmetrics](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/github.com/dholzmueller/probmetrics) and can be used seamlessly with any architecture. One limitation is that TS-refinement can be more sensitive to overfitting on small validation sets. In this case, cross-validation, ensembling, and regularized post-hoc calibrators could be useful. Another little-explored area is the influence of training parameters—such as optimizers, schedulers, and regularization—on the calibration and refinement errors during training, raising the question of how refinement-based early stopping should be integrated with these parameters to maximize efficiency. While refinement-based stopping is relevant in data-constrained settings prone to overfitting, it could also prove useful for the fine-tuning of foundation models, where training long past the loss minimum can be beneficial (Ouyang et al., [2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib46); Carlsson et al., [2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib10)). Additionally, while we explore its utility for model optimization, our refinement estimator could be a valuable diagnostic metric, especially in imbalanced multi-class settings where accuracy and area under the ROC curve are less appropriate.

Proper scoring rules have been used in meteorology to assess the quality of forecasts, see Gneiting & Raftery ([2007](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib20)) for an overview. They can also be motivated from a decision-theoretic point of view: The downstream loss for a decision-maker that chooses Bayes acts, i.e., actions that are optimal if the prediction is true, is a proper scoring rule (Grünwald & Dawid, [2004](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib25)). This construction also allows to properize non-proper scoring rules (Brehmer & Gneiting, [2020](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib7)).

For the Brier score (Brier, [1950](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib8)), the calibration-refinement decomposition was introduced by Sanders ([1963](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib54)) and the calibration-sharpness decomposition (see [Appendix B](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#A2 "Appendix B Calibration, Refinement, and Sharpness ‣ Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate")) was introduced by Murphy ([1973](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib41)). Bröcker ([2009](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib9)) generalized these decompositions to other proper scoring rules. Kull & Flach ([2015](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib32)) rewrite these decompositions purely in terms of divergences between different random variables and introduce more terms like irreducible, epistemic, and grouping loss. Pohle ([2020](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib50)) also provides alternative formulations. However, none of these formulations is variational.

Guo et al. ([2017](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib26)) observed that neural networks at their time were often miscalibrated and that logloss can overfit much earlier than accuracy, although the amount of miscalibration can depend on architectural and other details (Minderer et al., [2021](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib40); Tao et al., [2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib56)). Many post-hoc calibrations have been proposed to address this issue. Some methods are forms of logistic regression, as in Platt scaling (Platt et al., [1999](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib49)), Temperature/Vector/Matrix scaling (Guo et al., [2017](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib26)), Beta calibration (Kull et al., [2017](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib33)), and Dirichlet calibration (Kull et al., [2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib34)). Another family of methods stems from isotonic regression (Robertson et al., [1988](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib51); Zadrozny & Elkan, [2002](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib61); Oron & Flournoy, [2017](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib44); Vovk et al., [2015](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib58); Manokhin, [2017](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib38); Berta et al., [2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib3)). Approaches based on binning exist as well (e.g., Naeini et al., [2015](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib42)) but are perhaps more popular for estimating calibration errors. Wang et al. ([2021](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib59)) demonstrate that changing the loss function can improve calibration before, but not after post-hoc calibration.

Gruber & Buettner ([2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib23)) use a quantity similar to the loss for comparing post-hoc calibration methods, and Gruber & Bach ([2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib24)) propose a variational formulation for optimizing estimators of squared calibration errors. Ferrer & Ramos ([2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib18)) propose to look at the loss improvement through post-hoc recalibration as a measure of calibration error. The importance of optimizing the total loss and not only calibration error is emphasized, for example, by Perez-Lebel et al. ([2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib48)), Chidambaram & Ge ([2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib13)), and Ferrer & Ramos ([2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib18)). While we use a refinement estimator, Perez-Lebel et al. ([2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib48)) propose a grouping loss estimator that could be applicable in our case since the irreducible loss in our case is independent of ff. However, the grouping loss is harder to estimate than the refinement loss since a grouping loss estimator can be used to estimate the irreducible loss inffRisk⁡(f)\inf\_{f}\operatorname{Risk}(f).

Our analysis of classification and refinement errors for regularized logistic regression in the high-dimensional setting builds upon a rich literature. More specifically Dobriban & Wager ([2018](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib16)); Mai et al. ([2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib37)) study classification error with the same data model and provide asymptotic results that are directly applicable in our analysis. Couillet et al. ([2018](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib14)); Salehi et al. ([2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib53)) study adjacent scenarios that we experimented with. Bach ([2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib1)) provides a new perspective on these high dimensional results through the lens of self-induced regularization, that could prove relevant to interpret the formulas obtained for calibration and refinement errors.

children.heading: Remark B.3 (Extending the definitions of calibration, refinement, and sharpness).

content.text: [Theorem 2.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#S2.Thmtheorem1 "Theorem 2.1. ‣ 2.4 A variational formulation ‣ 2 Calibration-Refinement decomposition ‣ Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate") shows that for proper losses, calibration error is not only a divergence relative to a desired target (CC), but also a potential reduction in loss through post-processing. The latter perspective has been suggested by Ferrer & Ramos ([2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib18)) without showing equivalence to the former perspective. On the one hand, an advantage of the former perspective is that it extends to non-divergences like the L1L^{1} distance. On the other hand, an advantage of the latter perspective is that it can be used to extend the notion of calibration error, refinement error, and sharpness to non-proper losses (changing the desired target) or even non-probabilistic settings such as regression with MSE loss. Moreover, refinement error and sharpness can even be defined when f​(X)f(X) is not in the right space for the loss function, for example because it is a hidden-layer representation in a neural network. The variational formulation also allows to define more related quantities by using various function classes 𝒢\mathcal{G} and considering {IEEEeqnarray\*}rCl inf\_g ∈G Risk(g ∘f) . For example, considering the corresponding variant of calibration error for 1-Lipschitz functions, we obtain the post-processing gap from Blasiok et al. ([2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib5)). In the binary case, using increasing functions, we obtain the best possible risk attainable by isotonic regression.

heading_path: Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate
chunks.text:
###### Abstract

Machine learning classifiers often produce probabilistic predictions that are critical for accurate and interpretable decision-making in various domains. The quality of these predictions is generally evaluated with proper losses like cross-entropy, which decompose into two components: *calibration error* assesses general under/overconfidence, while *refinement error* measures the ability to distinguish different classes. In this paper, we provide theoretical and empirical evidence that these two errors are not minimized simultaneously during training. Selecting the best training epoch based on validation loss thus leads to a compromise point that is suboptimal for both calibration error and, most importantly, refinement error. To address this, we introduce a new metric for early stopping and hyperparameter tuning that makes it possible to minimize refinement error during training. The calibration error is minimized after training, using standard techniques. Our method integrates seamlessly with any architecture and consistently improves performance across diverse classification tasks.

## 1 Introduction

![Refer to caption](./[2501.19195] Rethinking Early Stopping_ Refine, Then Calibrate_files/x1.png)

Accurate classification lies at the heart of many machine learning applications, from medical diagnosis to autonomous driving systems. Modern classifiers predict not only a class label but also a probability vector reflecting the model’s confidence that the instance belongs to each class. This probabilistic output is critical for downstream decision-making. Despite their widespread use, many machine learning models, especially complex ones such as neural networks, tend to produce poorly calibrated probabilities (Guo et al., [2017](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib26)), meaning that the predicted confidence does not align with real-world probabilities.

This issue has mostly been considered through the lens of post-hoc calibration, which consists in adjusting the predicted probabilities after training, using a small held-out portion of the dataset. An overlooked aspect of the problem is that the calibration error contributes to the total loss of a classifier (Bröcker, [2009](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib9)). In [Figure 1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#S1.F1 "In 1 Introduction ‣ Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate") we plot the decomposition of the classification loss (here cross-entropy) into calibration error and refinement error during training for a deep neural network. We observe that the two are not minimized simultaneously. The resulting validation loss minimizer thus has a non-zero calibration error and is suboptimal for refinement. This observation reveals that there is room for improvement in the way we train machine learning classifiers.

In Sections [2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#S2 "2 Calibration-Refinement decomposition ‣ Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate") and [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#S3 "3 Our method: refinement-based stopping ‣ Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate") we propose minimizing only the refinement error during training and the calibration error after training. This new paradigm can be used seamlessly with any machine learning model by simply using our new refinement estimator, provided in the package [github.com/dholzmueller/probmetrics](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/github.com/dholzmueller/probmetrics), as a stopping metric. In [Section 4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#S4 "4 Experiments ‣ Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate"), we present empirical evidence of the loss reduction achieved across various problems. In Sections [5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#S5 "5 Decomposition in the Gaussian data model ‣ Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate") and [6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#S6 "6 High dimensional asymptotics of logistic regression ‣ Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate"), we study logistic regression on a binary Gaussian data model, demonstrating that the problem exists even in simple settings and that our method minimizes both refinement and calibration errors.

## 2 Calibration-Refinement decomposition

We begin by overviewing the decomposition of proper losses into calibration and refinement errors. We also present a new variational formulation of this decomposition that allows a reinterpretation of refinement as the loss after optimal post-processing.

### 2.3 Refinement error

Given the appeal of calibrated predictions, significant effort has been devoted to estimating and reducing calibration error. The fact that it interacts with another term to form the overall risk of the classifier, however, has received much less attention. This is partly due to the fact that refinement error is little known. So what exactly is refinement?

In decomposition ([1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#S2.E1 "Equation 1 ‣ 2.1 Proper loss decomposition ‣ 2 Calibration-Refinement decomposition ‣ Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate")), it appears as the expected ℓ\ell-entropy of YY given f​(X)f(X): ℛℓ​(f)=𝔼​[eℓ​(𝔼​[Y|f​(X)])]\mathcal{R}\_{\ell}(f)=\mathbb{E}[e\_{\ell}(\mathbb{E}[Y|f(X)])]. With simple intuition about entropy functions, we see that if YY is fully determined by f​(X)f(X), Y|f​(X)Y|f(X) has no entropy and the refinement error is null. In contrast, if Y|f​(X)Y|f(X) is as random as YY, it is maximal. chunks.text: ### 3.1 refinement-based early stopping: the intuition

heading_path: Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate
chunks.text:
#### Two distinct minimizers.

Minimizing the risk of a classifier comes down to minimizing simultaneously refinement and calibration errors. Empirically, these two errors are not minimized simultaneously during training, as in [Figure 1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#S1.F1 "In 1 Introduction ‣ Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate"). One possible scenario is that the training set becomes well separated, forcing the model to make very confident predictions to keep training calibration error small. In case of a train-test generalization gap, the model becomes over-confident (Carrell et al., [2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib11)) while refinement error might still decrease. We observe separate minimizers across various machine learning models, whether through iterative training or when tuning a regularization parameter. In [Section 6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#S6 "6 High dimensional asymptotics of logistic regression ‣ Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate"), we analyze this phenomenon theoretically for high-dimensional logistic regression, showing it appears even in very simple settings. The consequence is that risk-based early stopping finds a compromise point between two conflicting objectives: calibration error minimization and refinement error minimization. This corroborates the widely recognized observation that many models are poorly calibrated after training (Guo et al., [2017](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib26)).

heading_path: Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate
chunks.text:
#### Refine, then calibrate.

The question that arises is: how do we get a model optimal for both calibration and refinement? In general, strictly increasing post hoc calibration techniques like TS leaves refinement unchanged. Berta et al. ([2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib3)) showed that binary IR preserves the ROC convex hull, a proxy for refinement. Given that calibration error is minimized after training, with no impact on refinement, we argue that training should be dedicated to the latter only. We propose selecting the best epoch based on validation refinement error instead of validation loss as a new training paradigm for machine learning classifiers. As illustrated in Figure [2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3 Our method: refinement-based stopping ‣ Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate") this procedure leads to smaller loss after post-hoc calibration. Compared with the standard paradigm that minimizes both refinement and calibration during training, we propose refining during training, then calibrating post hoc.

#### Other estimators.

Our method applies to a wide range of machine learning models. It can help select the best step in any iterative training procedure (e.g, boosting) or the amount of regularization for non-iterative models. #### Computer Vision.

We benchmark our method by training a ResNet-18 (He et al., [2016](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib27)) and WideResNet (WRN) (Zagoruyko, [2016](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib62)) on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and SVHN datasets (Krizhevsky et al., [2009](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib31); Netzer et al., [2011](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib43)). We reserve 10% of the training set for validation. We train for 300 epochs using SGD with momentum, weight decay, and a step learning rate scheduler. We use random cropping, horizontal flips, and cutout (DeVries, [2017](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib15)). For reference, this training procedures allows us to reach 95%95\% accuracy on CIFAR-10 with the ResNet-18 and over 96%96\% with the WRN. We train the models ten times on each dataset. The code to run the benchmark is available at [github.com/eugeneberta/RefineThenCalibrate-Vision](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/github.com/eugeneberta/RefineThenCalibrate-Vision). After early stopping on validation loss (first column), using TS results in significant improvement (second column). Early stopping on TS-refinement instead of validation loss leads to even better results (third column). We also compare with validation accuracy based early stopping (fourth column), another refinement proxy, showing that TS-refinement more consistently yields smaller loss.

## 7 Conclusion

We have demonstrated that selecting the best epoch and hyperparameters based on refinement error solves an issue that arises when using the validation loss. We established that refinement error can be estimated by the loss after post hoc calibration. This allowed us to use TS-refinement for early stopping, yielding improvement in test loss on various machine learning problems. Our estimator is available in the probmetrics package [github.com/dholzmueller/probmetrics](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/github.com/dholzmueller/probmetrics) and can be used seamlessly with any architecture. One limitation is that TS-refinement can be more sensitive to overfitting on small validation sets. In this case, cross-validation, ensembling, and regularized post-hoc calibrators could be useful. Another little-explored area is the influence of training parameters—such as optimizers, schedulers, and regularization—on the calibration and refinement errors during training, raising the question of how refinement-based early stopping should be integrated with these parameters to maximize efficiency. While refinement-based stopping is relevant in data-constrained settings prone to overfitting, it could also prove useful for the fine-tuning of foundation models, where training long past the loss minimum can be beneficial (Ouyang et al., [2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib46); Carlsson et al., [2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib10)). Additionally, while we explore its utility for model optimization, our refinement estimator could be a valuable diagnostic metric, especially in imbalanced multi-class settings where accuracy and area under the ROC curve are less appropriate.

chunks.text:
#### Proper scoring rules.

Proper scoring rules have been used in meteorology to assess the quality of forecasts, see Gneiting & Raftery ([2007](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib20)) for an overview. They can also be motivated from a decision-theoretic point of view: The downstream loss for a decision-maker that chooses Bayes acts, i.e., actions that are optimal if the prediction is true, is a proper scoring rule (Grünwald & Dawid, [2004](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib25)). This construction also allows to properize non-proper scoring rules (Brehmer & Gneiting, [2020](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib7)).

#### Decompositions of proper scores.

For the Brier score (Brier, [1950](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib8)), the calibration-refinement decomposition was introduced by Sanders ([1963](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib54)) and the calibration-sharpness decomposition (see [Appendix B](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#A2 "Appendix B Calibration, Refinement, and Sharpness ‣ Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate")) was introduced by Murphy ([1973](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib41)). Bröcker ([2009](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib9)) generalized these decompositions to other proper scoring rules. Kull & Flach ([2015](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib32)) rewrite these decompositions purely in terms of divergences between different random variables and introduce more terms like irreducible, epistemic, and grouping loss. Pohle ([2020](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib50)) also provides alternative formulations. However, none of these formulations is variational.

chunks.text:
#### Calibration.

Guo et al. ([2017](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib26)) observed that neural networks at their time were often miscalibrated and that logloss can overfit much earlier than accuracy, although the amount of miscalibration can depend on architectural and other details (Minderer et al., [2021](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib40); Tao et al., [2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib56)). Many post-hoc calibrations have been proposed to address this issue. Some methods are forms of logistic regression, as in Platt scaling (Platt et al., [1999](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib49)), Temperature/Vector/Matrix scaling (Guo et al., [2017](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib26)), Beta calibration (Kull et al., [2017](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib33)), and Dirichlet calibration (Kull et al., [2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib34)). Another family of methods stems from isotonic regression (Robertson et al., [1988](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib51); Zadrozny & Elkan, [2002](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib61); Oron & Flournoy, [2017](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib44); Vovk et al., [2015](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib58); Manokhin, [2017](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib38); Berta et al., [2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib3)). Approaches based on binning exist as well (e.g., Naeini et al., [2015](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib42)) but are perhaps more popular for estimating calibration errors. Wang et al. ([2021](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib59)) demonstrate that changing the loss function can improve calibration before, but not after post-hoc calibration.

#### Post-hoc calibration and proper scores.

Gruber & Buettner ([2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib23)) use a quantity similar to the loss for comparing post-hoc calibration methods, and Gruber & Bach ([2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib24)) propose a variational formulation for optimizing estimators of squared calibration errors. Ferrer & Ramos ([2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib18)) propose to look at the loss improvement through post-hoc recalibration as a measure of calibration error. The importance of optimizing the total loss and not only calibration error is emphasized, for example, by Perez-Lebel et al. ([2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib48)), Chidambaram & Ge ([2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib13)), and Ferrer & Ramos ([2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib18)). While we use a refinement estimator, Perez-Lebel et al. ([2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib48)) propose a grouping loss estimator that could be applicable in our case since the irreducible loss in our case is independent of ff. #### High dimensional asymptotics of classification.

Our analysis of classification and refinement errors for regularized logistic regression in the high-dimensional setting builds upon a rich literature. More specifically Dobriban & Wager ([2018](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib16)); Mai et al. ([2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib37)) study classification error with the same data model and provide asymptotic results that are directly applicable in our analysis. Couillet et al. ([2018](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib14)); Salehi et al. ([2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib53)) study adjacent scenarios that we experimented with. Bach ([2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib1)) provides a new perspective on these high dimensional results through the lens of self-induced regularization, that could prove relevant to interpret the formulas obtained for calibration and refinement errors.

###### Remark B.3 (Extending the definitions of calibration, refinement, and sharpness).

[Theorem 2.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#S2.Thmtheorem1 "Theorem 2.1. ‣ 2.4 A variational formulation ‣ 2 Calibration-Refinement decomposition ‣ Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate") shows that for proper losses, calibration error is not only a divergence relative to a desired target (CC), but also a potential reduction in loss through post-processing. The latter perspective has been suggested by Ferrer & Ramos ([2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#bib.bib18)) without showing equivalence to the former perspective. On the one hand, an advantage of the former perspective is that it extends to non-divergences like the L1L^{1} distance. On the other hand, an advantage of the latter perspective is that it can be used to extend the notion of calibration error, refinement error, and sharpness to non-proper losses (changing the desired target) or even non-probabilistic settings such as regression with MSE loss. Moreover, refinement error and sharpness can even be defined when f​(X)f(X) is not in the right space for the loss function, for example because it is a hidden-layer representation in a neural network. The variational formulation also allows to define more related quantities by using various function classes 𝒢\mathcal{G} and considering {IEEEeqnarray\*}rCl inf\_g ∈G Risk(g ∘f) . For example, considering the corresponding variant of calibration error for 1-Lipschitz functions, we obtain the post-processing gap from Blasiok et al. #### Validation.

We are interested in minimizing the population risk of calibrated estimators. To faithfully estimate the population risk, it is possible to use cross-validation or the holdout method, fitting the calibrator on a part of the validation set while using its loss on the remaining part as a refinement estimate. However, we experimentally observe in [Figure G.2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#A7.F2 "In G.2 Other stopping metrics ‣ Appendix G Tabular experiments ‣ Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate") that fitting and evaluating temperature scaling on the entire validation set works equally well, perhaps because it only fits a single parameter. We use the latter approach in the following since it is more efficient compared to cross-validation.

### G.1 Dataset size dependency

[Figure G.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2501.19195#A7.F1 "In G.1 Dataset size dependency ‣ Appendix G Tabular experiments ‣ Rethinking Early Stopping: Refine, Then Calibrate") shows how the relative performance of refinement-based stopping vs logloss stopping depends on the dataset size. While the situation for small datasets is very noisy, for larger datasets the deterioration in the worst case is much less severe than the improvements in the best case. The advantages of TS-refinement become apparent at roughly 10K samples, which corresponds to a validation set size of 1,600. For XGB and MLP, there is one large outlier dataset where refinement-based stopping and logloss stopping both achieve low loss but the loss ratio is high.
